extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially speculative fiction) doing worldbuilding
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for creating and integrating worldbuilding into stories — what to design, how much to plan before drafting, and how to reveal setting details so they serve narrative, character, and theme. Focus is on novels/short fiction and on religions, culture, language, time systems, and spatial design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify axes of power
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the axes of power in the world: economic status, social hierarchies, etc., and which ones will your character intersect with in the story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the axes that affect your characters and the story. In short fiction, only a couple are likely to come into play — define those. Think in terms of narrative impact: which power structures shape movement, conflict, and choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include cultural detail only as narratively necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether cultural stuff is needed for the world to feel real, to provide conflict, or to impact characters' arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach worldbuilding from narrative needs rather than completeness. If a cultural element doesn't serve realism, conflict, or character development, consider omitting or minimizing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of cultural practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific practices embodied in the story; know where they come from and why they are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick concrete, particular cultural details rather than vague generalities. Understand the role a practice plays in society so you don't misrepresent or unintentionally insult when borrowing from real cultures. Specificity makes the world vivid and varied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful handling of religion (avoid monoliths)
rubrics_metrics.description: When depicting fictional religions overlapping with real ones, represent multiple viewpoints and avoid treating the faith as a single monolithic entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show intra-group diversity and how religion interweaves with other cultural parts. Portray individual experiences rather than summarizing or judging an entire group. Tell a person's story, not a story about a class of people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell specific characters' religious experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on a person who intersects with the religion rather than claiming to tell the story of the entire religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest characters with specificity and physicality so their relationship to faith reads as an individual perspective, reducing risk of broad, offensive generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layered worldbuilding (broad overview then dig in)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work in layers: build a broad overview first, then dig into details where needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frontload high-level structure when useful, but be prepared to research and invent in the 'recesses of your imagination' as you write. Patch and connect elements later; iterative revision is normal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frontload essentials but allow discovery writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do as much upfront planning as needed for the story, but accept that a lot will be discovered during drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the elements most likely to appear on the page so you can write varied descriptions; however, discovery writing and later retroactive fixes are acceptable and common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce worldbuilding tied to character conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: New worldbuilding elements should be introduced in connection with character conflict and development so they feel earned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If each reveal directly affects a character's crisis or growth, readers accept larger or later revelations. Use character stakes to justify world expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forewarn before an element matters (foreshadowing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce new elements slightly before they become important so they don't feel like last-minute contrivances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give readers hints or earlier references — ideally a couple of scenes or chapters ahead — so when the element is central it feels natural. Alternatively, introduce it earlier for a different reason and have it become relevant later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the world scene time and a personality
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want the world to feel like a character, name it and give it a personality; give the setting its own scenes apart from POV characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the environment acts like an antagonist, sidekick, or neutral force for the POV character. Allow the setting 'stage time' so it can be felt as an entity rather than mere backdrop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make setting influence plot and character decisions (setting agency)
rubrics_metrics.description: A setting becomes character-like when it influences plot choices and character behavior — i.e., when it has agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design spaces so their physical attributes constrain or enable actions (e.g., Bellagio in Oceans 11). If the world shapes movement, choices, and outcomes, it will feel active and consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design spaces deliberately to shape interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Be conscious of how built environments guide movement and interaction; deliberate design can create narrative constraints and opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study designed spaces (e.g., ships, public buildings) to see how layout promotes or inhibits certain behaviors; use that to craft scenes where place determines action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and vocabulary must match setting personality
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose descriptive vocabulary that fits the setting's character (e.g., words used to evoke New York differ from those for Disneyland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to the lexicon you use for environments; consistent, evocative word choice helps the reader perceive the setting's personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invent terminology sparingly and with purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Only create new calendar systems, units, currencies, or terms if they serve a meaningful story/cultural purpose; avoid overwhelming readers with unfamiliar words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some invented elements are more grokkable (currency context clues) than others (distance units). New terms should relate to your central metaphor and have histories and meanings. Too many invented words will confuse readers; be deliberate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure invented terms fit cultural/historical underpinnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that units, month names, and other terminology logically reflect the world's institutions (e.g., an 'Imperial inch' implies an empire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a term implies a past or social structure that doesn't exist in your world, change it or avoid invoking it. Use or avoid translated conventions (e.g., using 'October') depending on whether you want that historical implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary invention (use generic references when possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't have to invent replacements for every familiar term — sometimes it's easier to avoid naming (e.g., say 'summer' instead of inventing a new month name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a real-world term doesn't fit, you can often sidestep by describing function rather than renaming. This reduces reader friction while preserving world differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce worldbuilding elements for other narrative reasons to reduce telegraphing
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce elements initially for a different purpose so later revelations don't read as telegraphed exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a world element first appears for a minor or character-driven reason, its later significance will feel more organic than if it is clearly set up solely to serve plot twists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider how time is demarcated and culturally measured
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about calendars, markers (moon cycles, multiple moons), and how timekeeping shapes cultural practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if you don't explicitly use calendar mechanics in the story, considering time measurement can inform holidays, rhythms, and social organization. This can be part of off-page worldbuilding that affects on-page culture.
